Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

So there are a zillion of these, including ones that do what yours does. But that being said, I'm going to always upvote every single one of them because this is better and more important that what the big companies are doing across the board.

It feels like the last mile is so long in this space. I'm a SWE with a ton of experience and I still haven't gotten over the decision paralysis of figuring out which model to run locally, and which inference platform should I use, and will my M1 Macbook Pro actually run anything well enough to be useful, and on and on.

It's kind of embarrassing to admit, but having something Just Work(tm) makes getting started so much easier.

Shouldn’t be embarrassing to admit.

It’s a huge new subject area and it’s completely exhausting to learn. I still feel like a total novice.

I have an M1 Max (more memory bandwidth) so I am not sure how much advice I can give about models, but I would suggest maybe trying the new LFM2.5-24B-A2B. It’s surprisingly good. If you want to mess about with multimodal work, Gemma 4 12B is really impressive. (I mostly use Muse Glimmer but it might be rather slow on an M1 Pro)

If you want to have the space to learn the terminology, tinker with what you can control etc., then you have three easy options: LM Studio, Unsloth Desktop or the llama.cpp native Mac app. But don’t get put off by the llama.cpp command line; most of these tools are running it behind the scenes, and most entries on Hugging Face have recommended parameters.

MLX is an option but so far I haven’t found it to have an edge over simple GGUF on Metal on the M1 at least; it seems it might have more advantages on the later M series chips, but it is usually slower for me.

I have explored running OpenCode inside a VM (you can “remote into it” from the OpenCode GUi desktop app). You might want to look at Paseo, which can do a similar thing but with many more coding agents.

I am quite intrigued by Osaurus; on macOS 26 and up it looks like it will manage a container for you.

You might also want to look at Orchard. Not done this myself yet but I can see the appeal.

https://orchard.andon.dev/ai.html

I am an experienced web dev in my fifties. Six months ago everything I have written above would have been total gibberish to me. Learning some of the open weights stuff has made me feel much less helpless than I think I might if I just developed a Claude dependency. Nothing matters more to me than grasping the fundamentals.

I still don’t really use LLMs for hands-off coding. But I have found that a local LLM can be a useful sidekick; even at the most basic level it’s a better Google that remembers the context of queries.

Thanks for taking the time to write all this up, I'm checking out the projects you mentioned now.

I feel you on the tinkering-to-feel-less-overwhelmed front. I've been through a few ground shifts in my career so far, and even a little bit of "Oh, so that's how it works, ok..." can make it feel so much less daunting.

No worries. And yes, absolutely. Even the tiniest opportunity to poke around with stuff changes my perspective dramatically.

I've picked up lots of stuff this way — just being able to watch the server logs is great!

P.S. I prodded myself into playing with Osaurus; it's actually rather good.
Excellent, concise overview of stuff to explore—

Thanks :-)

Mostly I think my own approach has been to try to combat my anxiety and exasperation about all of this by taking this measure of control.

While no really small local model comes super-close to a frontier model, the shape of the technology is settling and I think one can learn so much by approaching it the conventional nerdy way: what's a practical setup I can run on kit I already have? What can I build that helps me explore the problems?

I am quite cynical about AI still, including for generative coding, but I am not cynical about what I can run locally. There is no doubt that they are already helpful to me even in a minimal form.

And the really cool thing about being able to run them locally is to understand the tradeoffs.
Definitely check out Osaurus for macOS and Windows. Heavily privacy focused with e2ee iOS and iPadOS tethers.

> Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install

Do you have examples of what hardware runs what models?

Here's roughly what it picks today from my testing:

- 8 GB Mac (M1/M2): Gemma 4 E2B

- 16 to 18 GB Mac: Gemma 4 E4B

- 24 to 64 GB Mac: Gemma 4 26B A4B

- 128 GB Mac Studio: gpt-oss 120B

- Windows/Linux with an RTX 3060 or 4070 (12 GB) and 32 GB RAM: Gemma 4 26B, split between the GPU and system memory

- RTX 4090: Gemma 4 26B fully on the GPU

- No GPU, 16 GB RAM: a compressed Gemma 4 E4B on the CPU

High level, it looks at your memory and memory bandwidth and then picks the smartest one that stays above about 15 tokens a second with room for a decent context.
